problem: Prior end-to-end RL navigation takes an explicit relative goal location; language-following work relied on parsing pipelines or a full-environment image, not partial egocentric observations. No end-to-end RL agent learned to follow free-form multi-step directions from partial views.
motivation: Humans navigate unknown places by following directions made of landmarks and turns. Robots that can follow such instructions could navigate in unseen situations. The observation is that the relevant part of an instruction changes as the agent moves, so attention conditioned on the current view should help.
key_idea: A DQN agent encodes the instruction with a bidirectional GRU and applies soft attention over its tokens, conditioned on the current semantic-segmentation and depth embeddings, to output discrete motion primitives.
insight: Attention conditioned on the visual context beats an identical network without attention: 30% relative more fully successful episodes on held-out instructions, and 13% fewer completely failed ones. Attention heatmaps show focus shifting over time, e.g. on 'left' when the agent turns left. Multi-step instructions remain hard: the agent never fully completes four- or five-step directions.
method: Problem formulation: POMDP on a 2D grid overlaid on SUNCG houses. Actions are turn pi/2, go straight and turn 3pi/2. The agent does not know its location or the goal.
Visual encoders: ground-truth semantic segmentation (3-layer CNN) and depth (2-layer CNN) are each embedded into a vector.
Language encoder: single-layer bidirectional GRU (32 units) over instruction tokens, giving per-token outputs o_i and final states h_F and h_B.
Conditioned attention: a feed-forward layer takes [v_S, v_D, h_B, h_F] and o_i, applies softmax over tokens, and forms an attention-weighted mean v_A, passed through FF to give v_L.
Q head: FF layers (16 and 8 units) over [v_S, v_D, v_L] output Q-values, trained with DQN and epsilon-greedy exploration.
Sparse waypoint reward: +1.0 for the final goal and +0.05 for each intermediate waypoint (given once); the episode ends at the goal or a step limit.
Baseline: identical network without the attention layer (CNN + RNN + FC).

setting.backbone: FollowNet: CNN + bi-GRU + feed-forward attention, trained from scratch with DQN
setting.training_data: 58 human-written instructions (7 tasks x 2 houses, forward and reversed) in 2 SUNCG houses, with about 5-10 random start nodes per task; 2.5M training steps
setting.observation: ground-truth semantic segmentation + depth from egocentric view + natural language instruction (no location)
setting.action_space: 3 discrete motion primitives on a 1 m grid: turn pi/2, go straight, turn 3pi/2
setting.privileged: ground-truth semantic segmentation and depth used as agent input; waypoints/goal areas used for reward only

numbers_note: Success numbers are macros (\devsuccess, \trainsuccess, etc.) whose values are not shown in the text, so exact figures are unavailable. Only relative claims are given: 30% relative increase in full success over the no-attention baseline, 13% relative decrease in complete failures, training-instruction success about 2% above evaluation. The custom 2-house dataset is not a canonical benchmark.
results: On 100 held-out two-step queries, FollowNet fully completes about 30% relatively more episodes than the no-attention baseline and has 13% relatively fewer total failures. On the training instructions from new start positions it does about as well, but never fully completes four- or five-step directions.
limitations: Tiny custom dataset (58 training instructions, 15 evaluation instructions, 2 houses) with limited vocabulary and no cross-house generalization
Uses ground-truth semantic segmentation and depth, and a discretized grid that assumes obstacle-free motion
Fails on long (four- or five-step) instructions; agent spins in place when it makes no progress
builds_on: Vision-and-Language navigation (Mei et al. / Misra et al.)
